findings.claim: The final couplet breaks from description into direct address. Having spent eleven lines observing the spectacle, the speaker suddenly turns to the reader
findings.problem: Slight internal inconsistency with the source text. The final couplet is lines 11-12 ('Beneath them sit the aged men, wise guardians of the poor. / Then cherish pity, lest you drive an angel from your door.'), and line 11 is still description; only line 12 turns to direct address. The lesson's own 'eleven lines of observing' figure confirms the shift happens in the final line, not across the whole couplet.
findings.correction: The final line breaks from description into direct address. Having spent eleven lines observing the spectacle — ending with the 'aged men, wise guardians of the poor' — the speaker suddenly turns to the reader

findings.claim: {"q": "What command opens the poem's final couplet?", "a": "'Cherish pity.'"}
findings.problem: Imprecise against the source text: the final couplet opens with the descriptive line 'Beneath them sit the aged men, wise guardians of the poor.' 'Then cherish pity' opens the poem's final line (the second line of that couplet), not the couplet.
findings.correction: {"q": "What command opens the poem's final line?", "a": "'Cherish pity.'"}

findings.claim: The final stanza returns to direct speech, breaking the narrating voice to let the flower speak. This closing shift from narration to personification gives the poem’s ending extra weight, since the poem’s last words are not the speaker’s own but the flower’s judgement on her life.
findings.problem: Contradicted by the source text of 'The Bluebell'. The flower's speech OPENS the final quatrain ('‘Sad wanderer, weep those blissful times / That never may return!’') and the poem then returns to the speaker's narration for its actual last two lines ('The lovely floweret seemed to say, / And thus it made me mourn.'). So the poem does not end on the flower's words, and the shift is from speech back to narration, not 'from narration to personification'. There is also no earlier direct speech for the stanza to 'return' to. A student asserting that the flower has the last word would be describing the poem inaccurately.
findings.correction: The final stanza breaks into direct speech, letting the flower speak first — ‘Sad wanderer, weep those blissful times / That never may return!’ — before the speaker’s voice closes the poem by reporting it: ‘The lovely floweret seemed to say, / And thus it made me mourn.’ The ending therefore gains its weight from the flower’s judgement being absorbed back into the speaker’s own grieving narration.

findings.claim: Each stanza rhymes loosely, with the first and last lines chiming and the third and fourth lines echoing each other — for example “face” and “going.”
findings.problem: The rhyme scheme is described wrongly. In the source text each stanza rhymes lines 2 and 5 (flame/came; string/thing; unknown/alone; above/of), giving an ABCDB pattern; line 1 ('boy') does not rhyme with line 5, and 'face' (line 3) does not rhyme with 'going' (line 4). What line 4 actually contains is an internal rhyme within the line itself ('knowing'/'going', 'gleams'/'beams', 'stake'/'undertake', 'in'/'find you in'). This is a mark-affecting AO2 error about form.
findings.correction: Each stanza follows the same pattern: the second and fifth lines rhyme (“flame”/“came”, “string”/“thing”, “unknown”/“alone”, “above”/“of”), while the first line of every stanza ends with the repeated phrase “journeying boy”. The long fourth line carries an internal rhyme inside itself — “Bewrapt past knowing to what he was going”, “twinkled gleams of the lamp’s sad beams” — so that the chime falls mid-line.

findings.claim: Gunn’s new-born “regrets” the change
findings.problem: Quotation not verbatim in the source text. 'Baby Song' reads 'I may sleep soon, I may forget, / But I won't forget that I regret.' The inflected form 'regrets' does not appear in the poem, so it must not sit inside quotation marks.
findings.correction: Gunn’s new-born insists “I won’t forget that I regret” the change

findings.claim: {"q": "Which two words show the boy doesn't understand his own past?", "a": "'Bewrapt past knowing.'"}
findings.problem: The question asks for two words but the answer quotes three ('Bewrapt past knowing'); the two-word phrase in the poem would be 'Bewrapt past'. The quoted phrase also refers to not knowing where he is going as well as whence he came, not only his past.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which phrase shows the boy understands neither where he is going nor where he came from?", "a": "'Bewrapt past knowing.'"}

findings.claim: The short sentence “So.” stands entirely alone after the hand is lost, breaking the poem’s flowing rhythm completely and marking the point where nothing can be undone.
findings.problem: Slight imprecision about the poem's layout. In the source text the word is not on a line of its own: the line reads 'So. But the hand was gone already.' It is a one-word sentence within a metrically short line, not a line standing entirely alone — a student repeating this as a structural claim could be marked as misreading the form.
findings.correction: The one-word sentence “So.” opens the deliberately short line “So. But the hand was gone already.”, interrupting the poem’s flowing rhythm and marking the point where nothing can be undone.

findings.claim: analysing how direct address and the closing claim that each is 'part of' the other unsettle a simple teacher-student hierarchy
findings.problem: 'Theme for English B' is a GUIDE ONLY poem in the source document: the complete list of quotable spans is 'I hear New York too', 'Bessie, bop, or Bach', 'instructor', 'true' and 'bop'. The span 'part of' is not on that list, so placing it inside quotation marks presents unverified wording as verbatim text (the idea appears only as OCR teacher-guide commentary: 'The speaker asserts that he is part of his instructor just as his instructor is part of him').
findings.correction: analysing how direct address and the closing claim that speaker and instructor are each part of the other unsettle a simple teacher-student hierarchy

findings.claim: When he insists “I hear New York too”, the short, direct statement challenges any assumption that Harlem is cut off from the rest of the city — the speaker belongs to both worlds at once. This works as a <dfn class="term" data-def="A question asked for effect rather than to get an answer, used to make a reader consider an issue rather than to invite a reply.">rhetorical question</dfn> being answered entirely on the speaker’s own terms.
findings.problem: As written, 'This' points back to the immediately preceding declarative statement 'I hear New York too', so the sentence labels a direct statement as a rhetorical question. The rhetorical question is the poem's opening query about whether the task is 'that simple', not this assertion — a terminology slip in an AO2-assessed section.
findings.correction: When he insists “I hear New York too”, the short, direct statement challenges any assumption that Harlem is cut off from the rest of the city — the speaker belongs to both worlds at once. It also answers, entirely on the speaker’s own terms, the <dfn class="term" data-def="A question asked for effect rather than to get an answer, used to make a reader consider an issue rather than to invite a reply.">rhetorical question</dfn> with which the poem opened.

findings.claim: The change is total: even colour and temperature reverse.
findings.problem: The poem contrasts the womb's warmth ('warm and wet and black') with light, noise and a 'rustling bed', but it never describes the world outside as cold; no temperature contrast appears in the text of 'Baby Song' (source text, OCR anthology). Only the light/dark and colour contrast is textually supported.
findings.correction: The change is total: light replaces darkness, and the baby that remembers being 'padded and jolly' now lies 'raging, small, and red'.

findings.claim: Perceptive analysis of the poem's opposing imagery of warmth and cold, dark and light, safety and noise, with precise quotation and sustained explanation of effect.
findings.problem: 'Cold' is not in the poem; Gunn gives the womb's warmth no cold counterpart, so rewarding 'warmth and cold' invites an unsupported claim about the text (source text, 'Baby Song').
findings.correction: Perceptive analysis of the poem's opposing imagery of warmth and exposure, dark and light, safety and noise, with precise quotation and sustained explanation of effect.

findings.claim: the baby moves from remembering ‘the private ease of Mother’s womb’ to describing how it fell ‘into the lighted room’
findings.problem: The poem's verb is present tense — 'I fall into the lighted room' — and the immediacy of that present tense is part of the poem's effect (source text, 'Baby Song', line 2). 'Fell' misreports the narrative tense.
findings.correction: the baby moves from remembering ‘the private ease of Mother’s womb’ to describing, in the present tense, how it falls ‘into the lighted room’

findings.claim: ‘You’re’ is written as a single, unbroken stanza of eighteen lines, with no verse breaks to mark stages of the pregnancy — instead, time passes only through the dates buried inside the list.
findings.problem: The form claim is wrong. Plath's 'You're' is eighteen lines arranged as TWO stanzas of nine lines each (the first stanza ends 'Farther off than Australia.' / the second begins 'Bent-backed Atlas, our traveled prawn.'). This is confirmed by published texts and analyses of the poem (Academy of American Poets text; eNotes and Poem Analysis both describe two stanzas of nine lines). The anthology source reproduces the text without printing stanza breaks, but the poem's actual form is two nine-line stanzas, and a structure answer built on 'one unbroken stanza' would be inaccurate.
findings.correction: ‘You’re’ is eighteen lines arranged as two nine-line stanzas, with the break falling after ‘Farther off than Australia.’ — the two halves of the poem mirror one another, and time passes not through verse breaks but through the dates buried inside the list.

findings.claim: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem's single unbroken stanza, its lack of a finite verb, and its debt to the riddle tradition, linking these choices convincingly to the poem's meaning.
findings.problem: Repeats the incorrect form claim: 'You're' is not a single unbroken stanza but two nine-line stanzas (verified against published texts of the poem, e.g. poets.org). Rewarding students for analysing a 'single unbroken stanza' would credit a factual error.
findings.correction: Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of the poem's two balanced nine-line stanzas, its lack of a main verb outside the title, and its debt to the riddle tradition, linking these choices convincingly to the poem's meaning.

findings.claim: Langston Hughes’s ‘Theme for English B’ shares Plath’s reference to the Fourth of July, though Hughes uses it to mark a different kind of new beginning — a young Black student finding his voice and identity in America.
findings.problem: 'Theme for English B' contains no reference to the Fourth of July (verified against the full text at poets.org and the OCR teacher-guide commentary, which records Winston-Salem, Durham, Harlem, the Y, 'Bessie, bop, or Bach' and 'I hear New York too', but no such date). The '(Fourth/Of July)' phrase in OCR's connections list belongs to Plath's 'You're', not to Hughes. Students building a comparison on a non-existent shared reference would lose marks.
findings.correction: Langston Hughes’s ‘Theme for English B’ offers a different kind of beginning — a twenty-two-year-old Black student in Harlem working out his identity on the page — so it contrasts usefully with Plath’s speaker, who must imagine an identity for someone who cannot yet speak for themselves.

findings.claim: The child is ‘Clownlike, happiest on your hands’ — a breech position rendered as circus acrobatics
findings.problem: The image describes the foetus head-down with 'Feet to the stars', which is the normal cephalic (head-first) presentation, not a breech position; breech means the baby is positioned feet or bottom first. Standard analyses of the poem read these lines as the head-down, feet-up position babies take before birth.
findings.correction: The child is ‘Clownlike, happiest on your hands’ — the usual head-down, feet-up position in the womb rendered as circus acrobatics

findings.claim: And Theresa Lola’s ‘Equilibrium’, which sets a birth against a grandfather’s decline, makes a striking contrast with Plath’s poem, which stays wholly, uncomplicatedly focused on the excitement of arrival, without death anywhere in view.
findings.problem: Misleading and contradicted by the poem and by OCR's own commentary. 'You're' invokes extinction and mortality in 'A common-sense / Thumbs-down on the dodo's mode' (which the lesson itself glosses as 'the extinct bird standing for failure to survive') and in 'moon-skulled'; OCR's teacher guide links 'You're' with 'Equilibrium' precisely as 'equations of birth and death'.
findings.correction: And Theresa Lola’s ‘Equilibrium’, which sets a birth against a grandfather’s decline, pairs revealingly with Plath’s poem: even at its most joyful, ‘You’re’ glances at mortality through ‘moon-skulled’ and the extinction implied by ‘the dodo’s mode’, so both poems hold new life and death in the same frame.

findings.claim: The poem never uses a finite verb of its own.
findings.problem: Slightly overstated: the poem does contain a finite verb inside a simile clause — 'Trawling your dark as owls do'. What is true is that the poem has no main verb of its own; every statement depends on the title's contracted 'You are'.
findings.correction: The poem has no main verb of its own outside the title.

findings.claim: The girl’s father takes her home “to a poor house” and the speaker’s father “watched her thrashed for almost drowning”.
findings.problem: Narrative detail wrong. The source text (and Poetry Archive / Clarke's own account in The Use of English) reads: 'My father took her home to a poor house / and watched her thrashed for almost drowning.' It is the SPEAKER'S father who both takes the child home and watches the beating; the girl's own father is never mentioned. The same error is repeated in this Key Fact's revision tip ('after the rescued girl's father takes her home').
findings.correction: The story does not end happily. The speaker’s father takes the rescued child home “to a poor house” and “watched her thrashed for almost drowning”. The heroic rescue and the harsh punishment sit side by side, with the poem making no comment — the reader is left to feel the injustice. (Revision tip: ‘Cover this and recall what the speaker’s father sees after he takes the rescued girl home.’)

findings.claim: before the poem’s harshest line arrives with no warning: her father “watched her thrashed for almost drowning”.
findings.problem: Same misattribution: the poem says 'My father took her home to a poor house / and watched her thrashed for almost drowning' — the watcher is the speaker's father, not the rescued girl's father.
findings.correction: before the poem’s harshest line arrives with no warning: the speaker’s father “watched her thrashed for almost drowning”.

findings.claim: After being rescued, the girl is later 'watched her _____ for almost drowning' by her father.
findings.problem: Factually wrong (the poem's watcher is the speaker's father, not the girl's father) and the stem is ungrammatical as a cloze.
findings.correction: The speaker's father takes the girl home to a poor house and 'watched her _____ for almost drowning.' (answer: thrashed)

findings.claim: {"q": "What happens to the rescued girl after her father takes her home?", "a": "He watches her 'thrashed for almost drowning.'"}
findings.problem: Misattributes the action: the source text reads 'My father took her home to a poor house / and watched her thrashed for almost drowning' — it is the speaker's father, not the girl's father.
findings.correction: {"q": "What happens to the rescued girl after the speaker's father takes her home?", "a": "He takes her to a poor house and watches her 'thrashed for almost drowning.'"}

findings.claim: The poem falls into two stanzas of uneven length. The first reads like a story told many times before; the second breaks that confidence apart, moving from short questions to long, hesitant clauses.
findings.problem: Form claim wrong. 'Cold Knap Lake' is printed in five stanzas of uneven length (4, 6, 4, 6 lines and a closing two-line rhyming couplet); Clarke's own essay on the poem refers to 'verse four' beginning 'Was I there?'. A wrong stanza count is mark-affecting in any structure question.
findings.correction: The poem falls into five stanzas of uneven length, closing on a two-line rhyming couplet. The opening stanzas read like a story told many times before; the questioning fourth stanza breaks that confidence apart, moving from the short question “Was I there?” to long, hesitant clauses before the couplet seals the poem.

findings.claim: The second stanza breaks the confident storytelling apart. The speaker suddenly asks “Was I there?”
findings.problem: 'Was I there?' opens the FOURTH stanza, not the second; the second stanza is the one describing the mother kneeling ('Then kneeling on the earth... my mother gave a stranger's child her breath'). Verified against the source text and Clarke's own account, which calls it 'verse four'.
findings.correction: The fourth stanza breaks the confident storytelling apart. The speaker suddenly asks “Was I there?”

findings.claim: The gap between the confident child-narrator of stanza one and the doubting adult voice of stanza two dramatises how memory itself ages and changes shape over time.
findings.problem: Repeats the wrong two-stanza structure: the doubting voice belongs to the fourth stanza and the final couplet, not to a 'stanza two'.
findings.correction: The gap between the confident narrative voice of the opening stanzas and the doubting adult voice of the fourth stanza and closing couplet dramatises how memory itself ages and changes shape over time.

findings.claim: The poem moves from a confident, dramatic story in stanza one to open doubt in stanza two, turning on the question “Was I there?”
findings.problem: Same structural error: the poem has five stanzas and 'Was I there?' opens the fourth, not a second stanza.
findings.correction: The poem moves from a confident, dramatic story in its opening stanzas to open doubt in the fourth, turning on the question “Was I there?”

findings.claim: {"q": "How many stanzas does 'Cold Knap Lake' have?", "a": "Two, of uneven length."}
findings.problem: Wrong count: the poem is in five stanzas of uneven length (4, 6, 4, 6 lines plus a closing rhyming couplet).
findings.correction: {"q": "How many stanzas does 'Cold Knap Lake' have?", "a": "Five, of uneven length, ending in a rhyming couplet."}

findings.claim: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the two-stanza structure, the volta at 'Was I there?' and the circular return to water imagery
findings.problem: Rewards a false structural fact: the poem has five stanzas, and the same error appears in the fifth question's descriptor ('Clarke's two-stanza shift from narrative to doubt'). A student following this guidance would assert a wrong stanza count in a structure answer.
findings.correction: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the five-stanza structure and its uneven verse lengths, the turn at 'Was I there?' opening the fourth stanza, the closing rhyming couplet and the circular return to water imagery (and, in the comparison question, 'Clarke's shift across stanzas from narrative to doubt').

findings.claim: the swans leave “heavy webs” that “beat and whistle on the air”
findings.problem: Misreads the poem: the source text has 'after the treading, heavy webs of swans / as their wings beat and whistle on the air' — it is the swans' WINGS that beat and whistle; the 'heavy webs' are their webbed feet treading the mud below.
findings.correction: the swans’ “treading, heavy webs” stir the mud below while “their wings beat and whistle on the air” above

findings.claim: The child’s near-death is softened by an unexpected simile: she is “dressed in water’s long green silk”
findings.problem: Terminology error that could cost AO2 credit: 'dressed in water's long green silk' contains no 'like' or 'as' — it is a metaphor, not a simile.
findings.correction: The child’s near-death is softened by an unexpected metaphor: she is “dressed in water’s long green silk”

findings.claim: as if drowning were almost beautiful, before the poem undercuts this with the shock of “blue-lipped”.
findings.problem: Reverses the order of the poem's line. The source text reads 'Blue-lipped and dressed in water's long green silk' — 'Blue-lipped' comes first and the beautiful image follows it, so the poem cannot 'undercut' the silk image with 'blue-lipped' afterwards.
findings.correction: as if drowning were almost beautiful — an image the poem has already braced with the shock of “Blue-lipped” at the head of the same line.

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the poem's final line about memory?", "a": "'All lost things lie under closing water.'"}
findings.problem: That is the penultimate line; the poem's final line is 'in that lake with the poor man's daughter'. The two lines together form the closing rhyming couplet.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which line in the closing couplet suggests memory is unrecoverable?", "a": "'All lost things lie under closing water.'"}

findings.claim: Clarke writes in <dfn class="term" data-def="Poetry that does not follow a regular rhyme scheme or metre, allowing rhythms closer to natural speech.">free verse</dfn>, with long, enjambed sentences that spill across line breaks
findings.problem: Broadly right but incomplete: the poem ends on a deliberate rhyming couplet ('closing water' / 'poor man's daughter'), which Clarke herself describes as a double-rhyming couplet. Students who claim the poem has no rhyme at all misdescribe its most obvious structural signal.
findings.correction: Clarke writes largely in free verse, with long, enjambed sentences that spill across line breaks the way a memory runs on without pausing — though the poem closes on a deliberate rhyming couplet (“closing water” / “poor man’s daughter”) that seals it like the ending of a fairy tale.

findings.claim: the newborn Olds spends her ‘first two weeks’ in hospital drinking whenever she wants — an ‘unlimited ration’ she later calls heaven
findings.problem: This contradicts the poem itself (source text, 'My First Weeks'): the hospital regime was NOT feeding on demand — 'Paradise / had its laws – every four hours and not / a minute sooner I could drink, but every four / hours I could have the world in my mouth.' What was unlimited was the QUANTITY at each feed, not the timing. The lesson's own later paragraph (n7) and flashcard ('How often could the newborn drink in hospital? Every four hours') both contradict this key fact, so students meet two incompatible accounts of the poem's central contrast. The real contrast is unlimited milk every four hours in hospital versus only 'four ounces of / water every four hours' at home.
findings.correction: The poem is built on one paradox: in her ‘first two weeks’ in hospital the timing was already strict — ‘every four hours and not / a minute sooner I could drink’ — but the amount was unlimited, so that at each feed she ‘could have the world in my mouth’, a ‘fortnight of unlimited ration’ she later calls heaven. Once home, the same four-hourly clock brings only ‘four ounces of / water’, and she ‘shrieked for it’ in between. Abundance turns into rationing within a fortnight.

findings.claim: enjambment — A pause or break within a line, or the running of a sentence past the end of a line without punctuation, which controls pace and can mimic natural speech or breath.
findings.problem: The first half of this definition describes caesura, not enjambment. Standard poetic-terminology sources (Poetry Foundation, Poetry Archive, OCR's own use of 'caesura' in the anthology teacher guide questions for 'Happy Birthday Moon' and 'Prayer') define enjambment solely as the continuation of a sentence or clause past the line end without terminal punctuation. Conflating the two terms risks students misusing subject terminology in an AO2-assessed answer. The identical wrong definition also appears in the <dfn> tooltip in content_html (n5) and must be corrected there too.
findings.correction: enjambment — The running of a sentence or clause past the end of a line or stanza without terminal punctuation, so the sense carries forward; it controls pace and can mimic natural speech or breath. (Distinguish from caesura: a pause or break within a line.)

findings.claim: For ‘My First Weeks’, a common mistake is describing the feeding routine without explaining what the paradox of abundance-then-rationing reveals about character.
findings.problem: Unevidenced assertion about typical candidate behaviour. The stated assessment rules (OCR J352 specification and sample paper/mark scheme) say nothing about common candidate errors on this poem, and no published OCR document is cited. Present the point as advice, not as a claim about what candidates commonly do.
findings.correction: For ‘My First Weeks’, make sure you do more than describe the feeding routine: explain what the paradox of abundance-then-rationing reveals about how the speaker’s character was formed.

findings.claim: who waves back so hard her ice-cream cone flies ‘through the air like a / butter-brickle cannonball.’
findings.problem: The poem says the ice cream, not the cone, flies: 'waved her cone back at me so / hard the ice cream flew through the air like a / butter-brickle cannonball'. The sister keeps hold of the cone.
findings.correction: who waves the cone back so hard that the ice cream itself flies ‘through the air like a / butter-brickle cannonball.’

findings.claim: {"q": "What image describes the sister's dropped ice cream flying through the air?", "a": "\"Like a butter-brickle cannonball.\""}
findings.problem: The poem does not say the ice cream was dropped; it flew off because the sister 'waved her cone back at me so / hard'. The stem states a detail the poem does not.
findings.correction: {"q": "What image describes the ice cream flying off the sister's waved cone?", "a": "\"Like a butter-brickle cannonball.\""}

findings.claim: she is reconstructing an origin story, using her mother’s account and her own imagination to explain her adult character
findings.problem: The poem never refers to a mother's account or to being told about her infancy; the source of the material is left unstated. This adds a narrative detail not in the text.
findings.correction: she is reconstructing an origin story, imagining rather than remembering her infancy in order to explain her adult character

findings.claim: while Olds’s speaker calls the same transition ‘Glorious life!’
findings.problem: In the poem 'Glorious life!' comes much later, after the move home and the water rationing, as the baby lies 'and moved my arms and legs like / feelers in the light' — it is not her reaction to leaving the womb. The lesson's own flashcard correctly glosses it as delight in moving her limbs, so the comparison paragraph is inconsistent with the text.
findings.correction: while Olds’s speaker treats her own emergence as effortless — ‘squeezed out / neatly into the cold illuminated / air and breathed it’ — and later exclaims ‘Glorious life!’ as she lies moving her limbs in the light

findings.claim: The broken, tumbling lines imitate a child’s unfiltered thought process: one idea leads straight into the next without the tidy punctuation an adult narrator might use. The lack of full stops across long stretches lets images collide — bank-sized flowers, silver bullets, and honey — exactly as they would in a five-year-old’s imagination.
findings.problem: This inverts the poem's actual punctuation. In the source text of 'Venus's-flytraps' the poem is dominated by short, heavily end-stopped declarative sentences, with full stops falling constantly and often mid-line ('Six-shooter. I can hurt', 'Babies come from. I am five.', 'All sticky & sweet inside.', 'I wonder what death tastes like.', 'Almost to Detroit.'). There are no 'long stretches' without full stops; the abrupt full stops, not their absence, are the poem's structural signature. A student writing this in an AO2 answer would be making a checkably false structural claim.
findings.correction: The broken, tumbling lines imitate a child’s unfiltered thought process: short lines and frequent enjambment (“I could start walking / & never stop”) pull one idea straight into the next. At the same time the poem is built from very short, blunt sentences whose full stops often fall in the middle of a line (“Six-shooter. I can hurt”; “Babies come from. I am five.”), so statements land abruptly and images collide — bank-sized flowers, silver bullets, honey — exactly as they would in a five-year-old’s mind.

findings.claim: Komunyakaa writes in free verse, with short, often single-line stanzas and frequent enjambment
findings.problem: The poem is not built from single-line stanzas; it runs as a continuous free-verse block of short lines with no regular stanza divisions. The 'single-line stanza' description is an imprecision about form that could mislead an AO2 structure comment.
findings.correction: Komunyakaa writes in free verse, as one continuous run of very short lines with frequent enjambment

findings.claim: {"q": "What poetic form and technique dominate the poem's structure?", "a": "Free verse with short lines and frequent enjambment."}
findings.problem: Breaches the flashcard rule that an answer must not be a list of items ('X, Y and Z'); three separate features (free verse, short lines, enjambment) are bundled into one card, and the question itself asks for two things at once. Each feature belongs on its own card.
findings.correction: Split into two cards: {"q": "In what verse form is 'Venus's-flytraps' written?", "a": "Free verse — no regular rhyme scheme or metre."} and {"q": "Which structural technique makes the boy's thoughts seem to tumble onwards?", "a": "Enjambment, as in ‘I could start walking / & never stop’."}

findings.claim: Then the speaker imagines him as royalty: “I thought he was an emperor,” “dying on silk cushions.” The simile is deliberately excessive.
findings.problem: Terminology error. In the source text the line is "I thought he was an emperor, / dying on silk cushions" — a direct equation with no 'like' or 'as', i.e. a metaphor, not a simile. Since the poetry section assesses AO2 (use of relevant subject terminology), mislabelling the device could cost marks if students reproduce it.
findings.correction: Then the speaker imagines him as royalty: “I thought he was an emperor,” “dying on silk cushions.” The metaphor is deliberately excessive.

findings.claim: She then builds an <dfn class="term" data-def="A comparison developed and extended across several lines, rather than stated once and dropped.">extended metaphor</dfn> around his hair, comparing it to the “vellum layer” of “some rare snowcreature’s” fur
findings.problem: Terminology error against the source text: the hair is described as "fine / as the innermost, vellum layer / of some rare snowcreature's / aureole of fur" — an explicit 'as' comparison, so this is an extended simile, not a metaphor.
findings.correction: She then builds an extended simile around his hair, describing it as “fine” as the “vellum layer” of “some rare snowcreature’s” fur

findings.claim: {"q": "What simile suggests the baby is fragile despite being called an emperor?", "a": "'Dying on silk cushions.'"}
findings.problem: The emperor image is a metaphor, not a simile ('I thought he was an emperor, / dying on silk cushions' — no 'like'/'as' in the source text). The card teaches the wrong AO2 term.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which phrase extends the emperor metaphor to suggest the baby's fragility in 'Love'?", "a": "'Dying on silk cushions.'"}

findings.claim: remember that the poetry section only rewards close reading of language, form and structure — there are no marks here for context or spelling and punctuation
findings.problem: Contradicts the stated assessment rules: the poetry section assesses AO1 as well as AO2, and part b) weights AO1 and AO2 equally. AO1 credits an informed personal response supported by textual reference, so it is wrong to tell students that only close reading of language, form and structure is rewarded. The 'no context / no spelling and punctuation marks' half of the sentence is correct.
findings.correction: remember that the poetry section rewards both a thoughtful personal response supported by well-chosen quotation (AO1) and close analysis of language, form and structure (AO2) — but there are no marks here for context or for spelling and punctuation

findings.claim: blurred and worn smooth as if by centuries of polishing
findings.problem: The source text reads "blurred / as if from years of polish" — 'years', not 'centuries'. The exaggeration misreports a detail of the poem.
findings.correction: blurred and worn smooth “as if from years of polish”

findings.claim: Plath also builds her poem about a baby entirely from chains of similes — “Clownlike”, “moon-skulled”, “Gilled like a fish”
findings.problem: Two of the three examples are not similes: in the source text 'Clownlike' and 'moon-skulled' are compound epithets/metaphors, while 'Gilled like a fish' is a simile. 'You're' is built from a mixture of metaphor and simile, not similes alone.
findings.correction: Plath also builds her poem about a baby entirely from chains of comparisons — metaphors such as “moon-skulled” and “my little loaf” alongside similes such as “Gilled like a fish”

findings.claim: His debut collection, The Perseverance (2016), was shortlisted for several poetry prizes and named on multiple books-of-the-year lists.
findings.problem: The publication year is wrong. The Perseverance was published by Penned in the Margins on 1 October 2018 (publisher page and London Review Bookshop listing, ISBN 9781908058522); it went on to win the Ted Hughes Award (2018) and the Rathbones Folio Prize (2019). The '2016' date reproduces an error in the OCR teacher guide and is off by two years.
findings.correction: His debut collection, The Perseverance (2018), won the Ted Hughes Award and the Rathbones Folio Prize and was listed among the books of the year.

findings.claim: {"q": "What is the title of Antrobus's debut poetry collection?", "a": "The Perseverance (2016)."}
findings.problem: Same date error: The Perseverance was published in 2018 (Penned in the Margins, 1 October 2018), not 2016.
findings.correction: {"q": "What is the title of Antrobus's debut poetry collection?", "a": "The Perseverance (2018)."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What phrase closes the poem, rewarding all its earlier repetition?", "a": "'Really hear each other.'"}
findings.problem: The phrase does not close the poem. As a pantoum the poem circles back at the end to its opening line about the father reading aloud while the speaker follows his finger across the page — OCR's own guide asks students how the change of punctuation on that returning final line alters its meaning. 'Really hear each other' occurs in the penultimate stanza, not as the closing phrase; telling students it is the last line risks a mark-costing structural error.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which phrase near the end of the poem signals genuine connection between father and son?", "a": "'Really hear each other'."}

findings.claim: Its speaker — recognisably the poet himself — remembers being born at the exact point his mother lay close to death from cancer.
findings.problem: Misleading narrative detail. The OCR teacher guide for 'Prayer' states that Kunial 'links his own birth to his mother's death' and 'uses this to remember the moment of his own birth as his mother lies on her deathbed' — i.e. the recollection of his birth happens at the deathbed decades later. As written, the sentence attaches 'at the exact point' to 'being born', implying the two events were simultaneous, which is not what the poem does.
findings.correction: Its speaker — recognisably the poet himself — stands at his mother’s deathbed as she nears death from cancer and, in that moment, remembers his own birth.

findings.claim: examiners want to see ideas and attitudes, tone and atmosphere, and the effects of language and structure discussed side by side
findings.problem: Unevidenced claim about examiner preference. The stated assessment rules confirm only that part a) carries three bullet points telling students what to consider (ideas and attitudes in each poem; tone and atmosphere in each poem; the effects of the language and structure used). Nothing in the specification or sample paper says examiners want balanced rather than sequential treatment, so the claim about what examiners want is a fabrication about examiner behaviour.
findings.correction: the question’s three bullet points direct you to ideas and attitudes in each poem, tone and atmosphere in each poem, and the effects of the language and structure used, so keep both poems in play as you work through each of those

findings.claim: analysing precise short quotations (such as Kunial's 'God's breath in man returning to his birth') alongside the unseen poem's methods
findings.problem: Wrong attribution of the quotation. 'God's breath in man returning to his birth' is George Herbert's line from 'Prayer (I)' (confirmed in Herbert's text via the Poetry Foundation), which Kunial alludes to; the OCR guide states 'Herbert speaks of' it. The lesson body attributes it correctly to Herbert, so this rubric contradicts the lesson and could lead students to present a borrowed line as Kunial's own writing.
findings.correction: analysing precise short quotations (such as Kunial's allusion to Herbert's 'God's breath in man returning to his birth') alongside the unseen poem's methods

findings.claim: A British poet born in Birmingham to an English mother and a Kashmiri father, known for blending English literary tradition with his Muslim and South Asian heritage.
findings.problem: Slight imprecision about whose faith tradition is in question. The OCR guide attributes the Muslim culture to Kunial's father ('links his father's diaspora Muslim culture to the English literary tradition'); it does not describe the poet's own religious identity.
findings.correction: A British poet born in Birmingham to an English mother and a Kashmiri father, known for blending the English literary tradition with his father's Kashmiri, Muslim heritage.

findings.claim: {"q": "Which single word ends Herbert's line that Kunial repeats as a quotable span?", "a": "Birth."}
findings.problem: The question uses internal editorial jargon ('quotable span') taken from the anthology support document, which is meaningless to a student and does not describe anything in the poem or exam; it also duplicates the content of the earlier Herbert-quotation card.
findings.correction: {"q": "Which word ending Herbert's borrowed line does Kunial also use in his own poem?", "a": "Birth."}

findings.claim: In 2016 her poetry featured in Beyoncé’s visual albums Lemonade and Black is King, bringing her writing to an audience far beyond the page.
findings.problem: Only Lemonade appeared in 2016. Black Is King premiered on Disney+ on 31 July 2020 (Disney/ABC press announcement; Variety, 2020), so dating both to 2016 is wrong by four years. (OCR's teacher guide repeats this slip, but the date is independently checkable and students should not learn it wrongly.)
findings.correction: Her poetry featured in Beyoncé’s visual albums Lemonade (2016) and Black Is King (2020), bringing her writing to an audience far beyond the page.

findings.claim: {"q": "In which year did Shire's poetry appear in Beyoncé's visual albums?", "a": "2016."}
findings.problem: The single date is wrong for one of the two albums: Lemonade is 2016 but Black Is King was released in July 2020 (Disney+/Variety). A card teaching '2016' for both embeds the error.
findings.correction: {"q": "In which year did Shire's poetry feature in Beyoncé's visual album Lemonade?", "a": "2016."}

findings.claim: The Somali words for grandmother, habooba and ayeeyo, sit inside the English of the poem rather than being translated away
findings.problem: Only 'ayeeyo' is Somali; 'habooba' (حبوبة) is Sudanese colloquial Arabic for grandmother, from the same root as 'love'. This also contradicts the source text, which lists the poem's languages as Arabic, Swahili and Welsh — Somali is not among the languages OCR names, so labelling both words 'Somali' misdescribes the poem's multilingualism.
findings.correction: The words for grandmother, habooba (Sudanese Arabic) and ayeeyo (Somali), sit inside the English of the poem rather than being translated away

findings.claim: {"q": "What are the Somali words for grandmother used in the poem?", "a": "Habooba and ayeeyo."}
findings.problem: Factually wrong ('habooba' is Sudanese Arabic, not Somali) and the answer is a two-item list, which the flashcard rules require to be split into separate cards.
findings.correction: Split into two accurate cards: {"q": "Which Somali word for grandmother does Shire use in the poem?", "a": "Ayeeyo."} and {"q": "Which Arabic word for grandmother does Shire use in the poem?", "a": "Habooba."}

findings.claim: {"q": "What does Shire say poetry helps her do to trauma?", "a": "Heal trauma."}
findings.problem: The answer simply restates the question ('do to trauma' → 'heal trauma'), which the flashcard rules prohibit; it also duplicates the ground covered by the neighbouring 'memory' card.
findings.correction: {"q": "What three purposes does Shire give for her poetry when she describes her aims?", "a": "Exploring memory, giving voice, and healing trauma."} — or, to keep one idea per card: {"q": "Why does Shire say she writes about painful family and refugee experience?", "a": "To heal, rather than simply record, that pain."}

findings.claim: Because this poem is not printed in full in the specification, you cannot rely on quoting long passages from memory.
findings.problem: Misleading reasoning about exam conditions. Per the stated assessment rules, J352/02 is a closed text examination and the anthology may not be taken in; for part b) the chosen anthology poem is not printed on the paper at all. The reason students cannot quote at length has nothing to do with what the specification prints.
findings.correction: Because this is a closed text examination and the anthology poem you choose for part b) is not printed on the paper, you cannot rely on quoting long passages from memory.

findings.claim: Early in the poem a startling simile catches new life and encroaching death inside the same image, unsettling the reader before the poem’s elegiac tone settles.
findings.problem: This misdescribes the poem's early simile. The OCR teacher guide (the only permitted source for this GUIDE ONLY poem) says only that the simile in line 4 is 'especially shocking' and gives no content; the actual poem's early simile compares the grandfather's silence after the naming ceremony to a body opened for a post-mortem — an image wholly of death and clinical stillness, not of new life and death combined. Students told the simile fuses birth and death will analyse an image that does not exist.
findings.correction: Early in the poem a shocking simile likens the grandfather's silence after the naming ceremony to a body opened for a post-mortem, treating the living man as though he were already a corpse and unsettling the reader before the elegiac tone settles.

findings.claim: in 2019 she was invited to read at the unveiling of Millicent Fawcett’s statue in Parliament Square
findings.problem: Date is wrong by a year. The Millicent Fawcett statue in Parliament Square was unveiled on 24 April 2018 (Mayor of London event listing; gov.uk record of the Prime Minister's speech at the unveiling, 24 April 2018), and Lola was commissioned by the Mayor's Office to write and read a poem at that 2018 ceremony. The OCR teacher guide repeats the 2019 error. The poetry section does not assess AO3, so no marks turn on this, but the date is checkably wrong.
findings.correction: in 2018 she was commissioned by the Mayor of London's Office to write and read a poem at the unveiling of Millicent Fawcett's statue in Parliament Square
